newsitem.title: USA: Reynolds lawyer says Fla case is about choice.
newsitem.headline: Reynolds lawyer says Fla case is about choice.

text.p: The key issue in a wrongful death lawsuit against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co was whether someone who chose to smoke "in the face of a barrage of anti-smoking messages" could then claim monetary damages, Reynolds attorney Paul Crist said in closing arguments Friday.

Crist told the six-member jury hearing a lawsuit brought by the family of late smoker Jean Connor that it needed only to decide the legal issues of whether Reynolds was negligent and had made a defective product.
Reynolds is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holding Corp.
"The issue in this case is not about sending messages," he said in the first half of his closing statement before court was dismissed for lunch.

Crist told the panel that Jean Connor had chosen to smoke despite a lifetime of warnings about the health risks, saying that no health issue in the history of the United States had commanded greater public attention.
"There is no obligation to warn people of that which they already know. That's the law," he said.

"There has been throughout this century and clearly throughout Jean Connor's lifetime, a widespread if not universal awareness that cigarette smoking is or may be hazardous to health," Crist said. "This is common knowledge."
Crist said the plaintiffs had failed in their legal responsibility to prove that there was a safer alternative product, and had not shown that Connor would have tried it and continued to use it.
He also said the warnings about potential health risks were legally adequate.
"Jean Connor was exposed to 27 years worth of warnings and chose to disregard them. Is it reasonable to suggest that an earlier or different warning would have made a difference to her?" he said.
Connor took up smoking as a teen-ager and eventually developed a three-pack-a-day habit. She died at age 49.

Crist also told jurors the suit was filed too late, arguing that Connor knew she had emphysema linked to smoking in 1982. In Florida, personal injury lawsuits must be filed within four years of the time that the injured party is aware of the injury.

Connor filed a liability suit against Reynolds in March 1995. She was diagnosed with lung cancer in 1993 and died in October 1995. Her sister Dana Raulerson refiled the suit as a wrongful death action on behalf of Connor's estate.
